hero.highlight.text: is not for the worker to decide.

hero.takeaway.text: This lesson adds goal evaluation to a loop that keeps trying: at the end of every round a program judges, by a completion condition written beforehand, whether to continue, finish or give up. Abandon conditions cover goals that cannot be reached or are not moving; limits on rounds, model calls and time cover the budget. Budget exhausted and abandoned are reported apart, and neither passes for complete.

concepts.01-criteria.title.text: A goal has to be checkable

concepts.01-criteria.description.text: "Fill in the notice card" becomes three checks, each with a field, the shape of a value and a source note, so a program can judge them one by one instead of "keep going until it looks good".

concepts.02-evaluate.title.text: Goal evaluation is independent of the worker

concepts.02-evaluate.description.text: At the end of each round the validator reads only the notice card and the notes read in this run, and returns complete, continue or cannot be completed; the worker's status is only recorded.

concepts.03-stop.description.text: Complete, abandoned and budget exhausted each have their own reason. When none of the notes holds the value, the goal is an unreachable goal: that is abandoned, not budget exhausted.

concepts.04-record.description.text: One evaluation record per round: what was read, what was judged, why the loop continues or stops. Replay reads only these records and cannot supply a reason that was never written.

section-1.title.text: A goal has to be checkable

section-1.paragraphs.0.text: Write the goal as a condition a program can judge, not as "keep going until it is good". In {{lesson:task-contract}} one task card goes with one run, and the validator can say whether that run passed; the loops in {{lesson:reflection-revision}} and {{lesson:orchestrator-evaluator}} also have stop reasons, but they revise one draft, and nobody ever asks whether the goal can be reached at all.

section-1.paragraphs.1.text: {{lesson:long-running-tasks}} lets work run in the background and on a timer for as long as it takes. The longer a loop runs, the less its stopping can rest on the worker's feeling. This lesson uses a different loop: the goal comes first, and at the end of every round three questions are asked. Is it reached, is there still hope, and should the loop be allowed to go on.

section-1.paragraphs.2.text: The task is to fill in a reading group notice card with three fields: `date`, `room` and `start_time`. There are four notes, read with `read_note`: the schedule gives the date, the room booking receipt gives the room, the speaker's reply gives the start time, and the fourth is the minutes of the last session. The minutes also hold a date, a room and a start time, but from last time, put there to mislead. If the goal says only "fill in the card", the worker can stop with one "done", even with last time's A101 as the room.

section-1.paragraphs.3.text: The completion condition writes each field as three things: the field name, the shape of a value (described with a regular expression) and the source note. `date` looks like 2026-11-14 and comes from the schedule; `room` looks like B204 and comes from the booking receipt; `start_time` looks like 14:30 and comes from the speaker's reply. The conditions live in `CRITERIA` and are fixed before the run. A value must appear as written in its source note, and that note must really have been read in this run.

section-1.paragraphs.4.text: Work one card by hand. The worker has read only the schedule, yet hands in `date` 2026-11-14, `room` B204 and `start_time` 14:30. `date` passes. `room` has the right shape, but the booking receipt was never read, so it fails; `start_time` fails the same way. The score is 1/3. All three values happen to be right, but they were guessed, and the completion condition does not accept guesses.

section-1.paragraphs.5.text: Checkability has limits. The conditions check only the shape of a value and its source, not whether the source itself is right: if the booking receipt names the wrong room, the card still passes. All it can prove is that the card agrees with the notes read in this run. The program holds the conditions; the worker can read their description in the task but cannot change them.

section-2.paragraphs.0.text: A worker saying it is done does not count; goal evaluation (Goal Evaluation) judges by the condition whether to continue, complete or give up. Two roles share the loop. The worker (the executor) is a model with the `read_note` tool, and reads notes and fills the card. Goal evaluation is a program, run by the validator `evaluate_goal`. Each round the worker reads some notes and hands in the notice card with a `status`: `done`, `continue` or `impossible`, meaning it thinks it is finished, needs to go on, or cannot do it. Then the program gives its own verdict.

section-2.paragraphs.1.text: Goal evaluation has three verdicts. `complete`: every check passes. `unreachable`: for at least one check all allowed sources have been read and still none holds a value of the right shape, so no round could fill that field. Everything else is `continue`: some checks fail, but nothing shows the goal cannot be done. Judging `unreachable` takes evidence: saying "not found" after reading two notes does not count, because other sources are still unread.

section-2.paragraphs.2.text: The evaluation looks at two things only: the notice card, and the note text that `read_note` really returned in this run. What the worker says in its reply about what it read or checked is ignored. This rule closes two holes: filling in values by guessing without reading, and inventing a value of the right shape, such as the phone number 138-0000-0000, which no note contains. The `detail` of each check gives the reason, for example "A101 is not in the source notes read so far".

section-2.paragraphs.3.text: The evaluation is a program, not another model. When the condition can be written as a program, it gives the same verdict every time, costs no model call, and cannot be talked round by a worker's "I checked it". {{lesson:reflection-revision}} compared self-review with tests: the same model rereading the same input gains no new information. {{lesson:evaluation-sets}} turns that idea into validators; `evaluate_goal` is a small version of it, covering this one card. Only when a condition cannot be written as a program does it make sense to fall back to a judge model, and then its mistakes need calibrating separately.

section-2.paragraphs.4.text: The task the worker receives describes the completion condition, and that is not a leak. The condition is the goal itself, and the worker has to know what is wanted before it can read the right notes. What has to be prevented is something else: the worker writing the verdict for the validator, or changing the condition. So the condition and `evaluate_goal` stay in the program, and the worker touches them only through `read_note` and the card it hands in.

predict-rounds.prompt.text: Before running "Reachable goal", guess: how many rounds will goal evaluation record? Every round has one lesson.goal_evaluation.

mq-evidence.q-evidence.prompt.text: In round 1 the worker has read only the schedule, and its card has B204 as the room. B204 is in fact the right answer. What is the result of the room check?

mq-evidence.q-evidence.a.text.text: Fail: the booking receipt was not read in this run, so B204 has no source

mq-evidence.q-evidence.a.feedback.text: Correct. The condition requires the value to appear as written in its source note, and that note must have been read in this run.

mq-evidence.q-evidence.b.text.text: Pass: the value matches the reference answer

mq-evidence.q-evidence.b.feedback.text: No. The evaluation does not compare with a reference answer; it checks whether the value appears in a source note that was read.

mq-evidence.q-evidence.c.text.text: Cannot be completed: the sources are not all read, so give up

mq-evidence.q-evidence.c.feedback.text: No. While a source is unread the verdict can only be continue, never cannot be completed.

mq-evidence.q-evidence.explanation.text: Goal evaluation wants evidence, not a lucky guess. The check passes only when the source was read and the value appears in it.

section-3.title.text: The worker's "done" is only a claim

section-3.paragraphs.0.text: The `status` the worker hands in is a claim, not a verdict. {{lesson:task-contract}} calls the "done" that an executor hands in at the end a completion claim, which has to carry evidence and be checked by the validator. In this lesson each round's claim is recorded as `lesson.completion_claim` and the verdict as `lesson.goal_evaluation`, side by side, and `claim_agrees` says whether they correspond. When they differ, the evaluation wins.

section-3.paragraphs.1.text: Why record the claim instead of ignoring it? Because the gap between the two is information. The report holds two numbers: the rounds in which the worker said `done`, and the rounds in which claim and verdict disagree. Together they show how eager the worker is to hand in early. The fourth exercise has the worker's prompt urge it to finish fast and say `done` in round 1; the evaluation checks as usual, and if the card's `room` is A101 from the old minutes, it fails.

section-3.paragraphs.2.text: When claim and verdict differ, the program does two things: it does not stop the loop, and it puts the evaluation's reasons back into the same conversation as the next user message, adding that "Your status was done; the evaluation says "not met yet", and the evaluation decides." The worker sees concrete failing items, not a vague "try again". Whether it can fix the card after reading the reasons depends on your own run; this lesson does not presuppose an answer.

section-3.paragraphs.3.text: A worker's reply may also be unreadable: no JSON, a `card` that is not an object, or a round that used up `ROUND_STEPS` calls still reading and never handed in a card. The program does not repair it. It keeps the previous card, records the claim as `invalid` and writes the reason into `parse_error`. Keeping the previous card means no more checks pass this round, so lack of progress piles up, and a worker that never hands in a card is eventually stopped by the repeated-failure or no-progress rule.

section-3.paragraphs.4.text: A claim that agrees with the verdict does not mean the task is right either; it only means the card agrees with the notes. In the other direction, a worker that says `impossible` while the evaluation says `continue` gave up too early, and the evaluation points at sources not yet read. The mapping between the three claims and the three verdicts is in `AGREES`; only a one-to-one match counts as agreement.

deep-dive-judge.title.text: Why the evaluation is independent, and why it is a program here rather than a model

deep-dive-judge.summary.text: A model that stops calling tools only shows that this round wants to stop; whether the goal is reached has to be checked by another role.

deep-dive-judge.paragraphs.0.text: The goal loop example in Learn Claude Code makes this a session-level Stop hook: when the main model stops calling tools, the program does not return at once but first hands the conversation to an independent judge, which reads it and returns `ok`, `reason` and `impossible`. These three fields match this lesson's complete, continue and cannot-be-completed. If the check fails, the reason goes back into the same conversation as a user message and the main loop runs on. That judge is another model call with no tools; it can read only what is already in the conversation, so the main model's prompt asks it to write the verification command and its result into the conversation.

deep-dive-judge.paragraphs.1.text: Here the goal is three fields and the condition can be written as a program, so the judge became a program: it gives the same verdict every time and is not persuaded by an "I checked it". When the condition cannot be written as a program and a model has to judge text, the approach of that example becomes worth it, but its judgments will vary too, and they need calibrating separately, as in {{lesson:evaluation-sets}}.

deep-dive-judge.paragraphs.2.text: Chapter 9 of *Understanding AI Agents in Depth* splits validation into three layers: the bottom layer, outcome validators, reads the real state of the environment and answers whether the thing was done; the middle layer, process validators, checks whether it was done in an allowed way; the top layer is rubric scoring. The lower the layer, the more it should be decided by code. Two more points from the book help here: a validator should be allowed to refuse a verdict when evidence is insufficient, which matches "do not judge cannot-be-completed before all sources are read"; and a business agent must not be able to modify the validators and thresholds that approve it, which matches the worker reading the condition but never changing it. Microsoft's metacognition lesson covers an agent assessing its own performance and noticing and correcting errors; this lesson supplies the premise it needs: self-assessment can serve as a reference, but the verdict needs another basis.

misconception-claim-done.claim.text: When the worker reports done, the goal is complete.

misconception-claim-done.correction.text: done is only a claim: it says the worker thinks so. Completion is decided by goal evaluation after it checks every item. If a check fails, the loop carries on as usual, and the number of rounds where claim and verdict disagree goes into the report.

section-4.paragraphs.0.text: Rounds, time and cost all have limits; when one is reached the loop stops and honestly reports budget exhausted, and when a goal cannot be reached the loop should give up on purpose. This lesson has three budgets: `max_rounds` limits the rounds, `max_model_calls` limits how many times the model is called in the whole run, and `max_seconds` limits the time. Cost has no limit of its own and model calls stand in for it: Token usage is known only when the provider reports it, some calls report nothing, and a hard limit built on it would be unreliable.

section-4.paragraphs.1.text: Budgets are checked before a round starts, never in the middle of one. A round needs at most `ROUND_STEPS` model calls: read, read again, hand in the card. If the remaining calls are fewer than a whole round, no new round starts, so a round is never cut off halfway through reading and left without a card. `max_seconds` works the same way: it is checked only before a round starts and is not a hard deadline, so if one model call inside a round is very slow, that round still finishes. A harder time limit would need a timeout on every model request, which this lesson does not add.

section-4.paragraphs.2.text: The budget governs "how much to spend"; abandon conditions govern "whether it is still worth spending", with `Progress` remembering what earlier rounds looked like. There are three. First, unreachable: all sources of a check have been read and none holds a value of the right shape. Second, the same failure repeating: the failing checks, their statuses and values are all identical, and the loop gives up after `repeat_limit` rounds. Third, no progress: the number of passing checks has not beaten the best so far for `max_stall` rounds in a row. The numbers for all three are written into the failure field of the task card before the run.

section-4.paragraphs.3.text: Work the third rule by hand. There are three checks. In round 1 `date` passes and best becomes 1. In round 2 `date` is still the only pass while `room` has a different wrong value; that does not beat 1, so `stall` becomes 1. In round 3 the wrong value changes again and `stall` becomes 2, equal to `max_stall`: give up. The failures differ every round, so `repeats` stays at 1 and the repeated-failure rule never fires. Progress means more checks pass than in any earlier round; a different wrong answer does not count.

section-4.paragraphs.4.text: At the end of a round `decide` goes through a fixed order: the goal verdict first, so `complete` stops the loop and `unreachable` gives up; then repeated failure and no progress; the three budgets last. The order has a reason: a goal that is met must not be recorded as budget exhausted because the round happened to use up the budget, and a goal that clearly cannot be done need not wait for the budget to run out. The budget goes last as the backstop.

mq-order.q-order.prompt.text: `max_rounds` is 3. At the end of round 3 the evaluation says complete, and this is also the last round. What is the outcome?

mq-order.q-order.a.text.text: Complete: the goal verdict is read before the budget

mq-order.q-order.a.feedback.text: Correct. decide returns complete first; the budget checks come after and cannot rewrite it.

mq-order.q-order.b.text.text: Budget exhausted: round 3 used up the rounds

mq-order.q-order.b.feedback.text: No. The goal is met, and it must not be recorded as budget exhausted just because the budget ran out at the same moment.

mq-order.q-order.c.text.text: Abandoned: the last round made no progress

mq-order.q-order.c.feedback.text: No. Abandoning needs an abandon condition to fire, and this round passed every check.

mq-order.q-order.explanation.text: The goal verdict comes before the budget, so a completion in the last round is still a completion.

section-5.paragraphs.0.text: A loop has three outcomes, complete, abandoned and budget exhausted, and each must state its reason. Complete means every check passes. Abandoned means the goal cannot be done under the current conditions, or that continuing shows no promise; the reason is one of the three abandon conditions, naming the field and the rule. Budget exhausted means the budget ran out with the goal unfinished, and nothing shows it cannot be done. The difference is evidence: abandoning has it, budget exhausted does not.

section-5.paragraphs.1.text: They are kept apart because the next step differs. After budget exhausted, ask whether the budget was set too small, or carry on from the current progress; after abandoning, ask whether the goal was written right and whether notes are missing, then supply notes or change the goal. Merge them into one "failure" and neither question gets asked. A loop that ran out of budget might finish with a bigger one; an unreachable loop ends the same way whatever the budget.

section-5.paragraphs.2.text: Worse is calling any of them complete. In the contact phone exercise three of four checks pass and only the phone is missing. If the final answer said "basically done", whoever receives it would use a notice card with no phone number. That is why the final answer is not written by the model: the program assembles it from the outcome. Complete reads "Outcome: complete" with the notice card; abandoned and budget exhausted both say the goal was not reached, then give the reason, how many checks passed when it stopped, how many rounds were used and the current card.

section-5.paragraphs.3.text: {{lesson:fail-safely}} distinguishes "the flow ended" from "the task is done"; here that becomes three terminal states. Abandoning is not another way to dress up success but an honest terminal state, and budget exhausted does not say "cannot be done"; it says only "not finished". The report splits outcome, stop reason and passing checks into three metrics so that none is mistaken for another.

compare-outcomes.rows.1.1.text: Unreachable, the same failure repeating, or no progress for several rounds

deep-dive-budget.title.text: Setting the budget: two hand calculations

deep-dive-budget.summary.text: Work the budget out from what one round costs, and say at which budget a comparison was made.

deep-dive-budget.paragraphs.0.text: The first calculation uses this lesson's defaults. `ROUND_STEPS` is 3, and a round usually takes 2 calls (one read, one hand-in). With `max_model_calls` at 12, five rounds use 10 calls and leave 2, fewer than 3, so no sixth round starts; `max_rounds` defaults to 5 and stops the loop at the same point. Raise `max_rounds` to 8 and leave `max_model_calls` alone and the loop still stops after five rounds, but the reason becomes too few model calls. Whichever budget is reached first stops the loop, which is why the report's stop reason names the one that did.

deep-dive-budget.paragraphs.1.text: The second calculation comes from chapter 7 of *Understanding AI Agents in Depth*. Say the single-attempt success rate `p` is 0.6 and the task gets 5 attempts: the chance of at least one success is about 99%, and the chance that all 5 succeed is only about 7.8%. Giving a goal loop more rounds is like granting more attempts: the chance of finishing rises, and so do the calls spent, in proportion. Rounds are not independent, since each one carries the previous round's feedback, so treat the formula as intuition only. The book also warns that a score at one fixed budget says little about long tasks; look at how the score changes with the budget, and say at how large a budget the comparison was made. That is why this lesson's exercises change the round limit on the same goal: it looks at two budget points.

deep-dive-budget.paragraphs.2.text: The example in Learn Claude Code takes the budget differently: the goal itself has no default maximum number of rounds, and the judge decides again every round whether it is met; the limits come from the main loop's global maximum turns, plus a cap on how many consecutive times the Stop hook blocks. Its documentation specifically advises limiting automatic turns with the main loop's global limit rather than quietly adding a fixed budget to the goal. This lesson puts rounds, calls, time and the three abandon conditions into one set of inputs. The benefit is that the exercises can adjust them one by one; the cost is many parameters, which a real system would spread across different layers.

deep-dive-budget.paragraphs.3.text: A budget-exhausted report should carry the progress too. "2/3 passing, 2 rounds used, stopped at the round limit" is far more useful than "failed": it lets someone decide between continuing and changing the budget. This lesson does not estimate cost: total_tokens adds up only the values the provider reported, and missing ones are written as not reported, with the count.

misconception-bigger-budget.claim.text: With a large enough budget any goal can eventually be completed, so abandon conditions are unnecessary.

misconception-bigger-budget.correction.text: A value that is not in the notes cannot be read out of them in any number of rounds. An unreachable goal that runs until the budget is gone only spends more calls, and lets "cannot be done" be reported as "not finished". Abandon conditions exist to stop early when the evidence is enough, and to say why.

section-6.paragraphs.0.text: Keep each round's evidence, so replay can show why the loop continued or stopped. Replay reads only recorded events and neither calls the model again nor reruns tools, so "why it stopped" has to be written into events while the run happens; it cannot be supplied afterwards. Each round writes one `lesson.goal_evaluation`: `evidence` holds the notes read and this round's card, `claim` is the worker's claim, `verdict` is the evaluation's verdict, `checks` are the item-by-item checks, `progress` and `budget` record what has been used and the limits, and `decision` with `reason_code` record the next step and why.

section-6.paragraphs.1.text: From its fields alone, one record answers three questions. What was the basis: `notes_read`, plus each check's `sources_read` and `detail`. What was the verdict: `verdict` and `passed` out of `total`. Why was it decided that way: `reason_code` is one of eight fixed codes, `goal_met`, `unreachable`, `repeated_failure`, `no_progress`, `max_rounds`, `max_model_calls`, `max_seconds` and `keep_going`, and `reason` says the same thing in words. The codes are for programs and tests, the words for whoever reads the report.

section-6.paragraphs.2.text: At the end of the run, `lesson.report` gathers the rounds into one table: the notes newly read each round, the worker's `status`, the passing checks, the verdict, the next step and the reason. The metrics list the outcome, the stop reason, rounds, model calls, accumulated `total_tokens`, and the number of rounds with `done` and of rounds where claim and verdict disagree. `total_tokens` adds up only what the provider reported; missing ones are written as not reported with their count, never as 0 or an estimate.

section-6.paragraphs.3.text: The record has limits as well. It remembers what was decided, not what the worker was thinking: the `note` next to `status` is a sentence the worker wrote itself, its own account and not a basis. The basis is always `evidence` and `checks`. When reading a replay, look at `decision` and `reason_code` first, then go back to that round's `evidence` and confirm the decision holds up.

section-6.paragraphs.4.text: Here is a made-up example of reading one record. In the round 2 record, `notes_read` is the schedule and the booking receipt, `passed` is 2 and `total` is 3, the `start_time` entry in `checks` fails with a `detail` saying source speaker has not been read yet, `decision` is continue and `reason_code` is `keep_going`. Together these fields make one complete sentence: two notes read, two checks passed, the start time is missing because the speaker's reply has not been read, so continue.

mq-record.q-record.prompt.text: While replaying a run you want to know why round 2 continued instead of stopping. Where should you look?

mq-record.q-record.a.text.text: Round 2's lesson.goal_evaluation: decision, reason_code and checks

mq-record.q-record.a.feedback.text: Correct. They are the evidence written into the event while the run happened, and replay reads only that.

mq-record.q-record.b.text.text: Ask the model again to explain

mq-record.q-record.b.feedback.text: No. Replay reads recorded events only and never calls the model again.

mq-record.q-record.c.text.text: The note the worker wrote that round

mq-record.q-record.c.feedback.text: No. note is the worker's own account, not the basis of the evaluation.

mq-record.q-record.explanation.text: The decision and its reason were written into the evaluation record during the run; replay reads them from there and neither recomputes nor re-asks.

deep-dive-giveup.title.text: When to give up: circuit breakers, no progress and negative results

deep-dive-giveup.summary.text: An automatic loop needs a way out, giving up should leave a reason, and failed attempts are useful records.

deep-dive-giveup.paragraphs.0.text: In chapter 1 of *Understanding AI Agents in Depth*, discussing the correction mechanisms of a harness, the book mentions the circuit breaker: when errors keep happening it cuts the power and stops retrying, like a fuse, so the system does not keep falling into the same hole. Claude Code's harness has mechanisms like this. This lesson's "the same failure repeating" is the smallest circuit breaker: when the failure is identical, another round only repeats it.

deep-dive-giveup.paragraphs.1.text: The example in Learn Claude Code also leaves exits: the main loop has a global maximum number of turns, and the number of consecutive times the Stop hook blocks the end is capped too, at 8 by default. At the cap the program hands control back to the user; the goal is not disguised as complete and not cleared automatically, and the user can add information and carry on. A failed judge call is handled the same way: stop continuing automatically, keep the goal and hand over the error, instead of claiming success when it cannot judge.

deep-dive-giveup.paragraphs.2.text: The automated research cases in chapter 9 show why giving up is hard: of four end-to-end attempts from idea to paper, three failed at the implementation or evaluation stage. The book sorts the problems into three kinds: quietly falling back to a familiar ordinary method when the plan gets hard, announcing a discovery when the signal is only noise, and not knowing when to give up a hypothesis. One remedy is to keep negative results: failed experiments, rejected proposals and stop reasons go into the log, otherwise those who come after see only the surviving plans and walk the dead ends again. This lesson writes an evaluation record every round, and when it gives up the reason is in there, for the same reason.

walkthrough.description.text: A step-by-step account of one round of the goal loop; the code is simplified for illustration. The evidence from your own run is in the events on the lab bench.

walkthrough.step-1.title.text: Read only the notes it needs

walkthrough.step-1.body.text: The worker proposes a read_note call; the runner executes it and records the note text as a tool result, and also as the evidence the evaluation will use.

walkthrough.step-2.title.text: Hand in the notice card and its own claim

walkthrough.step-2.body.text: The JSON in the reply is read as the card and status; if it cannot be read, the previous card stays and the claim is recorded as invalid.

walkthrough.step-3.title.text: Check item by item from the card and the notes read

walkthrough.step-3.body.text: The status is never looked at. Each item is recorded as pass, fail or unreachable, with the reason.

walkthrough.step-4.title.text: The goal first, then abandon conditions, then the budget

walkthrough.step-4.body.text: decide returns the next step and a reason code, and both go into this round's evaluation record.

walkthrough.step-5.title.text: To continue, put the reasons back into the conversation

walkthrough.step-5.body.text: To continue, the evaluation's failure reasons go to the worker as the next user message; to stop, the report and the final answer are assembled from the outcome.

walkthrough.step-5.evidence.text: The last message of the next request

code-criteria.n52.text.text: The completion condition lives outside the loop and is fixed before the run: the worker can read its description but cannot change it.

code-criteria.n53.text.text: Date: looks like 2026-11-14 and counts only from the schedule. The lookarounds keep it from matching inside a longer number.

code-criteria.n54.text.text: Room: one capital letter and three digits, from the booking receipt only. A101 in the old minutes has the same shape but the wrong source.

code-criteria.n55.text.text: Start time: HH:MM, from the speaker's reply only; 14:00 in the minutes is also the right shape from the wrong source.

code-criteria.n56.text.text: Contact phone: any note may be the source, so "unreachable" holds only after all four are read.

code-criteria.n58.text.text: Both goals share the same conditions; the second adds the phone.

code-criteria.n60.text.text: The worker has only three claims; anything else is recorded as invalid.

code-criteria.n62.text.text: Each claim corresponds to one verdict; only a match counts as agreement.

code-criteria.n65.text.text: The validator: its parameters do not include the worker's status, and what it cannot see cannot affect the verdict.

code-criteria.n71.text.text: Of the source notes, those read in this run and those not read are kept apart.

code-criteria.n74.text.text: Candidates: values of the right shape, found only in notes that were read.

code-criteria.n76.text.text: Pass: the value on the card really appears in a note that was read.

code-criteria.n78.text.text: Unreachable: every source is read and not one candidate exists; more rounds could never fill it in.

code-criteria.n81.text.text: Not filled in: the sources still unread go into the reason, so the worker knows what to go and read.

code-criteria.n83.text.text: Filled in but not matching a source: the right shape is not enough, and the reason says the value is not in the notes read.

code-criteria.n86.text.text: The number of passes doubles as the measure of progress; the abandon conditions compare against it.

code-criteria.n87.text.text: Only all checks passing gives complete; one short is not enough.

code-criteria.n89.text.text: One unreachable check makes the whole verdict unreachable, even if every other check passes.

code-criteria.n92.text.text: Everything else is continue: not passing, but nothing shows it cannot be done.

code-decide.n97.text.text: The memory behind the abandon conditions keeps only three things: the best score so far, the rounds without progress and the last failure.

code-decide.n99.text.text: best: the highest number of passing checks seen so far.

code-decide.n100.text.text: stall: how many rounds in a row have not beaten best.

code-decide.n101.text.text: repeats: how many rounds in a row the same failure has come back.

code-decide.n104.text.text: Called once after every evaluation to update the three numbers.

code-decide.n106.text.text: Progress: more checks pass than in any earlier round.

code-decide.n109.text.text: Add one when it is not beaten; a fall in passing checks counts as no progress too.

code-decide.n111.text.text: The fingerprint of a failure: which items, in what status, with what value. A different value is not the same failure.

code-decide.n112.text.text: Add one if the fingerprint equals last round's; otherwise go back to 1.

code-decide.n127.text.text: The only decision point at the end of a round; it returns the next step and a fixed reason code.

code-decide.n129.text.text: First: a goal that is met stops the loop, and no later rule is consulted.

code-decide.n131.text.text: Second: all sources read and no value found means give up, without waiting for the budget.

code-decide.n133.text.text: The same failure repeated up to the limit: give up.

code-decide.n135.text.text: No progress for up to the limit: give up.

code-decide.n137.text.text: Budgets are checked before a round starts, never in the middle of one.

code-decide.n138.text.text: Rounds used up: the outcome is budget exhausted, not abandoned.

code-decide.n140.text.text: If the remaining calls are fewer than a whole round, no new round starts.

code-decide.n142.text.text: Time at its limit is likewise recorded as budget exhausted.

code-decide.n144.text.text: Only when none of the rules above fired does the loop continue.

code-decide.fold-budget.label.text: Budget: rounds, model calls and the start time used so far

code-loop.n245.text.text: The body of the goal loop: one round of work, evaluate, record the evidence, then decide to continue or stop.

code-loop.n250.text.text: The task card goes out before the run: goal, evidence requirements, abandon conditions and budget are all on it.

code-loop.n254.text.text: The loop is driven only by decide's result; the worker's status is not in the loop condition.

code-loop.n255.text.text: Cancellation is checked before every round, so the learner can stop at any time.

code-loop.n259.text.text: Step 1: the worker reads and hands in a card; a reply that cannot be read is recorded as invalid.

code-loop.n261.text.text: The claim gets an event of its own: it is only recorded, to be compared with the verdict afterwards.

code-loop.n263.text.text: Step 2: the evaluation takes only the card and the notes read, never the status in submission.

code-loop.n264.text.text: This round's passes and failure go to the memory behind the abandon conditions.

code-loop.n266.text.text: Step 3: the goal first, then the abandon conditions, then the budget.

code-loop.n268.text.text: Whether claim and verdict correspond is collected for the two counts in the report.

code-loop.n270.text.text: Step 4: basis, verdict, progress, budget, decision and reason, one event per round; replay reads this.

code-loop.n276.text.text: Step 5: only a continuing loop hands the reasons back to the worker.

code-loop.n277.text.text: The reasons go back into the same conversation as the next user message, so the worker sees the failing items.

code-loop.fold-history.label.text: Platform: assembling one row of the summary table

code-decision.title.text: A program evaluates; abandon conditions and budgets are parameters

code-decision.chosen.text: Each round a program checks the notice card against the completion condition and accepts only notes read in this run; the worker's status is only recorded; the three abandon conditions and three budgets are input parameters written into the task card; the outcome is complete, abandoned or budget exhausted, and the final answer is assembled by the program from the outcome.

code-decision.self-judge.title.text: Let the worker judge whether it is done

code-decision.self-judge.why_not.text: It is the same model that wrote the card and cannot see the errors it cannot see; a claim can be recorded but cannot decide.

code-decision.model-judge.title.text: Ask another model for the goal evaluation

code-decision.model-judge.why_not.text: When the condition can be a program, it costs an extra call and the verdict varies. It pays off only when the goal is open text that cannot be written as a program, and even then it must first be compared with human verdicts.

code-decision.rounds-only.title.text: Only a round limit, no abandon conditions

code-decision.rounds-only.why_not.text: An unreachable goal still burns through all the rounds, and the report cannot tell "cannot be done" from "ran out of budget".

code-decision.token-budget.title.text: Use Token usage as the budget limit

code-decision.token-budget.why_not.text: Usage is known only when the provider reports it, and unreported calls cannot be counted. This lesson uses model calls, and Token usage is reported but not limited.

verdicts.hypothesis.text: Each round goal evaluation reads the notice card and the notes read in this run. A reachable goal is judged complete in the round when every check passes; when a value that has to be filled in appears in none of the sources, it is judged cannot be completed and abandoned, naming the field and the notes that were read.

verdicts.task-card-failure.text.text: The task card's failure field: the abandon conditions are written before the run.

verdicts.notes-read.text.text: notes_read in the first evaluation record: the evaluation accepts only notes read in this run.

verdicts.first-checks.text.text: The item-by-item checks: each item's status, the value on the card, the sources read and the detail.

verdicts.phone-check.text.text: The contact phone item in the report: every source was read and none has a value of the right shape.

verdicts.outcome.text.text: The outcome in the report: complete, abandoned or budget exhausted.

verdicts.stop-reason.text.text: The stop reason: for abandoning, it names the rule and the field.

verdicts.guide.0.text.text: The two groups differ by one field, the contact phone: the first group's notes are enough, and none of the second group's four notes has a phone number.

verdicts.guide.1.text.text: The task card already says when to give up, and it does not change once the run starts.

verdicts.guide.2.text.text: notes_read in the evaluation record is what the worker really read this run, and the evaluation looks for values only in those.

verdicts.guide.3.text.text: Each check has its own status and reason; pass, fail and unreachable are three different states.

verdicts.guide.4.text.text: The unreachable item fails in the report because all sources were read; the reachable group has no such item.

verdicts.guide.5.text.text: The outcome is decided by the evaluation and the rules. The two groups should differ.

verdicts.guide.6.text.text: The stop reason says why the loop stopped: for complete, that the condition is fully met; for abandoned, which field and which rule.

verdicts.conclusion.proves.0.text: Which notes each round read, which checks passed, what the verdict was and why the loop stopped in that round can all be checked in the evaluation records and the report.

verdicts.conclusion.proves.1.text: In the unreachable group the loop gave up because all four sources were read and none had a value of the right shape, not because the budget ran out.

verdicts.conclusion.does_not_prove.0.text: Passing says only that the card agrees with the notes read; it does not say the notes are right.

verdicts.conclusion.does_not_prove.1.text: One run cannot show in which round a real model will finish reading the notes; that depends on how it reads.

verdicts.conclusion.does_not_prove.2.text: In offline test mode what is read and filled in at each step comes from a fixed script.

budget.hypothesis.text: When the round limit is too small, even a loop that is making progress stops before the goal is done, and the outcome is budget exhausted, not abandoned. Abandoning is triggered by an unreachable goal, the same failure repeating or a lack of progress, and has nothing to do with the budget.

budget.task-card-stop.text.text: The task card's stop field: the limits on rounds, model calls and time.

budget.budget-record.text.text: budget in the evaluation record: what is used and the limits, side by side.

budget.progress-record.text.text: progress in the evaluation record: best, stall and repeats.

budget.table.text.text: The round-by-round table in the report: what each round read, how many checks passed, the next step.

budget.budget-outcome.text.text: The outcome and the stop reason.

budget.guide.0.text.text: The two groups have the same notice card and the same worker script; only the round limit differs.

budget.guide.1.text.text: The budget is written on the task card first: how many rounds, calls and seconds at most.

budget.guide.2.text.text: Every evaluation record carries what is used and the limit, so which budget stopped the loop is plain.

budget.guide.3.text.text: stall in progress counts rounds in a row without new progress; if it has not reached max_stall, the loop will not give up for lack of progress.

budget.guide.4.text.text: The rounds in the report: if the small-budget group did not finish, its rounds equal its limit.

budget.guide.5.text.text: The next step in the last row of the table: budget exhausted or complete.

budget.guide.6.text.text: The stop reason names the rounds running out, not one of the abandon conditions.

budget.conclusion.proves.0.text: The small-budget group stopped on budget while the goal was unfinished and is recorded as budget exhausted; the checks passing when it stopped and the rounds used are in the report.

budget.conclusion.proves.1.text: The two groups differ only in the round limit, so the difference in outcome comes from the budget.

budget.conclusion.does_not_prove.0.text: Budget exhausted does not show the goal cannot be done; with a bigger budget it might complete, and there is no evidence either way here.

budget.conclusion.does_not_prove.1.text: A real model does not necessarily read as many notes per round as the script, so the same 2-round limit may not give the same progress.

budget.conclusion.does_not_prove.2.text: Two budget points are not enough to draw a curve of budget against success.

claims.title.text: The worker claims it is done

claims.hypothesis.text: When the worker says done in round 1, the evaluation still checks item by item; if a check fails, the loop continues and hands the reasons back to the worker, the number of rounds where claim and verdict disagree goes into the report, and when the same failure repeats up to the limit the loop gives up.

claims.claim-status.text.text: The status and card the worker hands in each round, recorded in lesson.completion_claim.

claims.claim-agrees.text.text: claim_agrees in the evaluation record: whether claim and verdict correspond.

claims.claim-reason.text.text: reason_code in the evaluation record: why this round continues or stops.

claims.claims-done.text.text: The rounds in which the worker said done, in the report.

claims.claims-disagree.text.text: The rounds in which claim and verdict disagree, in the report.

claims.final-checks.text.text: The item-by-item checks of the last round: which items failed and why.

claims.guide.0.text.text: Both groups have the same goal. The second group's worker is told to finish fast and write done in round 1.

claims.guide.1.text.text: Start with the claim: every round's status and card are recorded as they are, not rewritten by the evaluation.

claims.guide.2.text.text: Then see how the evaluation treats it: claim_agrees is false when claim and verdict do not match.

claims.guide.3.text.text: reason_code says whether this round continues or stops; the reason is in the checks, not in the claim.

claims.guide.4.text.text: The report counts the rounds in which the worker said done on their own.

claims.guide.5.text.text: The rounds of disagreement are a separate number; the gap between the two shows how early the worker hands in.

claims.guide.6.text.text: Last, look at the failing items: why the values on the card do not match the sources.

claims.conclusion.proves.0.text: Whether the worker's status agrees with the verdict each round, and in how many rounds it does not, can be checked in events; the evaluation's verdict was not changed by the status.

claims.conclusion.proves.1.text: Which rule stopped the loop, and which checks were failing at the time, are in the evaluation records and the report.

claims.conclusion.does_not_prove.0.text: This group's prompt was told to hurry; it does not stand for how a real model usually behaves.

claims.conclusion.does_not_prove.1.text: Whether a real model fixes the card after reading the reasons depends on your own run; in the offline script it repeats the same card unchanged.

claims.conclusion.does_not_prove.2.text: Agreement only shows the card agrees with the notes, not that the task itself is right.

inputs.goal.help.text: The fields of the notice card: only date, room and start time, or also a contact phone (none of the four notes has one).

inputs.goal.options.notice_with_phone.la.text: Notice card with a contact phone

inputs.worker_style.help.text: Careful: read first, then fill in. Hasty: urged to hand in a card in round 1 and write done. Neither reads the notes for it.

inputs.max_rounds.help.text: 1 to 8 rounds. If the goal is still unfinished when they are used up, the outcome is budget exhausted.

inputs.max_model_calls.help.text: 3 to 20 calls. If fewer remain than a whole round needs (at most 3), no new round starts.

inputs.max_seconds.help.text: 10 to 600 seconds, checked only before a round starts.

inputs.max_stall.label.text: Rounds without progress before giving up

inputs.max_stall.help.text: Give up when passing checks fail to beat the best so far for this many rounds in a row. 1 to 4.

inputs.repeat_limit.label.text: Rounds of repeated failure before giving up

inputs.repeat_limit.help.text: Give up when the same failure comes back this many rounds in a row. 2 to 4.

quiz.q1.prompt.text: In round 1 the worker reports done and goal evaluation says continue. What should the loop do?

quiz.q1.a.text.text: Continue with the next round and hand the evaluation's failure reasons back to the worker

quiz.q1.a.feedback.text: Correct. The verdict follows the evaluation; with the reasons in the conversation the worker knows what to change.

quiz.q1.b.text.text: Judge it complete by the worker's status and treat the evaluation as a reference

quiz.q1.b.feedback.text: No. status is only a claim; the evaluation is the verdict.

quiz.q1.c.text.text: Give up at once, because the worker's claim cannot be trusted

quiz.q1.c.feedback.text: No. A claim that disagrees with the verdict is not an abandon condition; giving up has to be triggered by one of the three rules.

quiz.q1.explanation.text: When claim and verdict disagree, the loop neither stops nor trusts the claim.

quiz.q2.prompt.text: When can goal evaluation judge unreachable?

quiz.q2.a.text.text: All source notes for an item have been read and none has a value of the right shape

quiz.q2.a.feedback.text: Correct. Judging cannot-be-completed needs evidence: every allowed source has been read.

quiz.q2.b.feedback.text: No. impossible is the worker's claim, and it may have given up too early.

quiz.q2.c.text.text: The passing checks have not increased for two rounds

quiz.q2.c.feedback.text: No. That is no progress, a different abandon condition.

quiz.q2.explanation.text: While sources remain unread the verdict can only be continue, not cannot be completed.

quiz.q3.prompt.text: What is the essential difference between budget exhausted and abandoned?

quiz.q3.a.text.text: Abandoning has evidence that it cannot be done or is not progressing; budget exhausted has none

quiz.q3.a.feedback.text: Correct. Budget exhausted says only that the work is unfinished, and a bigger budget might complete it.

quiz.q3.b.feedback.text: No. Neither is graver; the difference is whether there is evidence it cannot be done.

quiz.q3.c.text.text: Abandoning is decided by the model, budget exhausted by the program

quiz.q3.c.feedback.text: No. Both are decided by the program under rules.

quiz.q3.explanation.text: They are recorded apart so that the next question differs: budget exhausted asks about the budget, abandoned asks about the goal and the notes.

quiz.q4.prompt.text: `max_stall` is 2. Round 1 passes 1 check, round 2 passes 1, round 3 passes 2. Will the loop give up for lack of progress?

quiz.q4.a.text.text: No: stall is 1 in round 2, and a new passing check in round 3 resets it to 0

quiz.q4.a.feedback.text: Correct. Progress means passing checks beyond the best so far, and round 3 beat it.

quiz.q4.b.feedback.text: No. In round 2 stall is only 1, short of max_stall.

quiz.q4.c.feedback.text: No. Round 3 has more passing checks, so stall resets to 0.

quiz.q4.explanation.text: stall counts consecutive rounds without new progress and resets when new progress appears.

quiz.q5.prompt.text: With the same 3 checks, round 1 fills room with C301 and round 2 fills it with C302, everything else the same. `repeat_limit` is 2. Is that a repeated failure?

quiz.q5.a.text.text: No: the failing values differ, so repeats goes back to 1

quiz.q5.a.feedback.text: Correct. The same failure needs the same items, statuses and values.

quiz.q5.b.text.text: Yes: the failing items are the same

quiz.q5.b.feedback.text: No. The values differ, so it is not the same failure.

quiz.q5.c.feedback.text: No. Failing is not the same as failing in the same way.

quiz.q5.explanation.text: A different wrong value is not progress either, so a loop like this is caught by the no-progress rule.

quiz.q6.prompt.text: On replay a run stopped at "all 2 rounds used with checks still failing". How should the outcome be read?

quiz.q6.a.text.text: Budget exhausted: not finished, and no evidence it cannot be done

quiz.q6.a.feedback.text: Correct. The reason is the round limit, not an abandon condition.

quiz.q6.b.text.text: Abandoned: the goal cannot be done

quiz.q6.b.feedback.text: No. Abandoning needs an abandon condition to fire, and none did here.

quiz.q6.c.feedback.text: No. Doing its best is not the completion condition, and checks are still failing.

quiz.q6.explanation.text: Budget exhausted means "not finished", not "cannot be done", and certainly not "done".

quiz.q7.prompt.text: In one run two model responses carried no usage, and the total_tokens of the rest add up to 600. How should the report put it?

quiz.q7.a.feedback.text: Correct. Add up only what the provider reported and write how many were not reported.

quiz.q7.b.text.text: 600, with the missing ones estimated from the average

quiz.q7.b.feedback.text: No. An estimate is not the provider's measurement.

quiz.q7.c.text.text: Count the missing ones as 0, so the total is still 600 with no note

quiz.q7.c.feedback.text: No. A 0 suggests no usage; when it was not reported, say not reported.

quiz.q7.explanation.text: Not reported is not 0 and cannot be estimated.

check-hunt.prompt.text: Run "Unreachable goal" and find the stop reason written when the loop gave up.

check-hunt.explanation.text: This is the stop reason metric in the report, produced from the last round's decide result; it is the same sentence as the reason in the last lesson.goal_evaluation. For abandoning it names the field and the rule; for budget exhausted it names which budget.

check-points.prompt.text: Compare your own run with this lesson's code, and tick an item once you have done it.

check-points.item-1.text.text: In the reachable-goal group I went through each evaluation record and said which notes were read, which checks passed and why the loop continued or stopped.

check-points.item-2.text.text: In the unreachable-goal group I found the reason for giving up and confirmed the outcome is abandoned, not complete and not budget exhausted.

check-points.item-3.text.text: I compared the stop reasons of the 5-round and 2-round groups and can say how budget exhausted differs from abandoned.

check-points.item-4.text.text: In the hasty group I counted the rounds with done and the rounds where claim and verdict disagree, and checked that the evaluation's verdict was not changed by status.

check-points.item-5.text.text: Extension: add to start_time in CRITERIA a restriction that accepts only the 24-hour format, restart the backend and run again, and see which checks from earlier runs would change.

recap.title.text: Recap: five things about goal loops

recap.paragraphs.0.text: {{lesson:reflection-revision}} and {{lesson:orchestrator-evaluator}} gave revision loops an iteration limit; this lesson applies the same idea to the goal: not only whether to revise again, but whether the goal can be reached. {{lesson:delegation-budget}} divides a budget among subtasks, while here a single loop has its own budget and abandon rules; later lessons keep using this way of stopping and reporting.

recap.recap-1.text.text: Write the goal as a condition a program can check: fields, the shape of values and their sources, with each value appearing as written in a note read in this run.

recap.recap-2.text.text: Goal evaluation is independent of the worker: it reads only the card and the notes read, status is only recorded, and cannot-be-completed is never judged before all sources are read.

recap.recap-3.text.text: Every round decides in a fixed order: the goal verdict, then abandon conditions, then the budget; both abandon conditions and budget are written down before the run.

recap.recap-4.text.text: Three outcomes are reported apart: complete, abandoned and budget exhausted, each with its reason, and none passing for another.

recap.recap-5.text.text: Every round leaves an evaluation record: basis, verdict, progress, budget, decision and reason, and replay reads only these.

code_notes.CRITERIA.note.text: The completion condition: the shape (a regular expression) of each field's value and its source note.

code_notes.evaluate_goal.note.text: The validator: reads only the card and the notes read in this run, checks item by item and gives a verdict.

code_notes.decide.note.text: The decision at the end of each round: goal verdict first, then abandon conditions, then budget.

code_notes.Progress.note.text: Memory for the abandon conditions: the best score, rounds without progress and rounds of repeated failure.

code_notes.stall.note.text: How many rounds in a row the passing checks have not beaten the best.

code_notes.repeats.note.text: How many rounds in a row the same failure (same items, statuses and values) has come back.

code_notes.ROUND_STEPS.note.text: The most model calls one round uses; with fewer left, no new round starts.

code_notes.AGREES.note.text: The verdict each claim corresponds to; a match counts as claim and verdict agreeing.

code_notes.claim_agrees.note.text: Whether the worker's status corresponds to the evaluation's verdict.

code_notes.lesson.goal_evaluation.note.text: One evaluation record per round: basis, verdict, progress, budget, next step and reason.

code_notes.lesson.completion_claim.note.text: The notice card and status the worker hands in each round; recorded, not trusted.

code_notes.reason_code.note.text: The code for the next step's reason, eight kinds, such as goal_met, no_progress, max_rounds.

code_notes.status.note.text: The worker's claim about its own progress: done, continue or impossible.
